title: China and Pakistan Move to Build a South Asian Bloc Without India
excerpt: With SAARC dormant for over a decade, Beijing and Islamabad are courting Bangladesh and other neighbours for a new regional grouping that sidelines New Delhi.
body:
• China and Pakistan held trilateral talks with Bangladesh in Kunming in June 2025 to lay groundwork for a new South Asian regional bloc that could replace SAARC
  • SAARC has not held a summit since 2014, paralysed by the India-Pakistan standoff over terrorism and the 2016 Uri attack boycott
  • India faces a strategic squeeze as neighbours recalibrate ties with Beijing, but analysts say any bloc without New Delhi lacks the economic heft to succeed

For nearly twelve years, the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation has existed only on paper. No summits, no ministerial rounds, no movement on the customs union or free-trade area that its eight members once envisioned. Now China and Pakistan are trying to fill that vacuum — with a new grouping that would leave India on the outside looking in.

In June 2025, senior diplomats from China, Pakistan and Bangladesh met in Kunming to discuss forming a regional bloc focused on trade, infrastructure and connectivity, according to reports in The Express Tribune and India Today. It was the second such trilateral meeting China hosted — the first brought together Beijing, Islamabad and Kabul. India was excluded from both.

A Decade of Paralysis

SAARC was founded in 1985 with the ambition of becoming South Asia's answer to ASEAN or the EU. Its eight members — India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Nepal, Bhutan, the Maldives and Afghanistan — account for nearly a quarter of the world's population. But the organisation has been held hostage by the India-Pakistan rivalry almost from the start.

The last formal summit took place in Kathmandu in 2014. When India pulled out of the planned 2016 summit in Islamabad after the Uri terror attack, Bangladesh, Bhutan and Afghanistan followed suit. No summit has been scheduled since.

India shifted its diplomatic energy toward sub-regional alternatives: BIMSTEC, the Bay of Bengal grouping that includes Thailand and Myanmar but excludes Pakistan, and the BBIN framework linking Bangladesh, Bhutan, India and Nepal on motor-vehicle and trade agreements.

Beijing's South Asian Playbook

China has moved into the gap with a combination of infrastructure lending, arms sales and diplomatic courtship. Bangladesh now sources roughly 72 percent of its military equipment from China, according to the Dhaka Tribune. The China-Pakistan Economic Corridor, the $62 billion flagship of the Belt and Road Initiative, is being extended toward Afghanistan and Central Asia.

Bangladesh's political transition in 2024, which replaced the India-aligned Sheikh Hasina government with an interim administration under Muhammad Yunus, has accelerated the shift. Yunus has pursued warmer ties with both Beijing and Islamabad, while relations with New Delhi have cooled.

"China may see a regional vacuum with a non-functional SAARC, but it is unlikely to succeed in filling the gap with another regional entity."

— Anuradha Chenoy, Adjunct Professor, O.P. Jindal Global University

The smaller South Asian states are hedging. Nepal, sandwiched between India and China, participates in BRI projects while maintaining visa-free arrangements and deep trade dependence on India. The Maldives carries over $3 billion in Chinese debt but has recently moved to strengthen ties with New Delhi. Sri Lanka, still recovering from its 2022 economic crisis, balances between Indian and Chinese investment while servicing IMF loan conditions.

India's Dilemma

New Delhi faces a bind largely of its own making. By refusing to engage with Pakistan through SAARC, India effectively froze the region's only multilateral forum. The resulting vacuum has given China space to court India's neighbours bilaterally — and now collectively.

A 2026 paper in The Round Table journal noted that "the promise of the transforming potential of geo-economics is now buried under geopolitical imperatives in which terrorism has taken centre stage" — a dynamic that has become a make-or-break moment for SAARC's future.

Indian officials have expressed concern about the Kunming meetings, viewing them as a deliberate attempt to reshape South Asian alignments. But the proposed bloc faces its own structural problem: without India's $3.5 trillion economy — which dwarfs the combined GDP of all other SAARC members — any new grouping lacks the economic gravity to drive meaningful regional integration.

What This Means for the Diaspora

For the Indian diaspora, a fractured South Asia complicates everything from family travel to business investment. Dormant SAARC visa regimes, suspended trade corridors and shifting diplomatic winds all affect cross-border movement and commerce. Indians working in the Gulf and Southeast Asia who maintain ties across South Asian borders are watching these realignments closely — any new bloc could reshape visa policies, trade routes and remittance corridors that millions depend on.

What's Next

Pakistan and China plan to invite Sri Lanka, the Maldives and Afghanistan to join the proposed grouping. India would receive a formal invitation but is not expected to accept. Whether the bloc materialises depends on whether smaller nations are willing to join a formation that alienates the region's largest economy.

For India, the strategic imperative is clear: either revive a credible multilateral forum or watch China assemble one without it. As Chenoy wrote, India "cannot allow regionalism, trade and related issues to be held hostage on account of the zero-sum game with Pakistan." The question is whether New Delhi is willing to pay the political price of engagement.
